results.title: Past, Present and Future With p-Values, Confidence Intervals and Effect Sizes - The Journal of Foot and Ankle Surgery
results.content: The main tools used to make inferences in the frequentist framework are *p*-values, effect size, and confidence intervals (CI). A *p*-value is usually calculated in the context of null hypothesis significance testing (NHST) (1). With continuous data, the researcher may use the Student's *t* test to determine a test statistic, which is associated with a certain *p*-value. Based on the *p*-value, the researcher may decide to reject or not reject the null hypothesis that the groups have equal means. The *p*-value indicates the probability of detecting a more extreme test statistic or more extreme data than that already observed (1). Another way is to see that the *p*-value describes how compatible the data are with the null hypothesis and other background assumptions (2). Assume, for example, that the researcher obtained a *p*-value of .13 for the group difference using the Student´s *t* test. This means, assuming that the null hypothesis and all the background assumptions are true, that a *p*-value of .13 indicates that there is 13% chance that the researcher would detect a difference larger than that observed if the study was repeated. In practice, 95% CIs are inherently associated with the *p*-value if a *p*-value of .05 is used as the criterion for statistical significance. Another very common misconception is the assumption that a nonsignificant *p*-value indicates that the null hypothesis is true. If we obtain a *p*-value below the predefined cutoff, say, .05, it means that we have evidence against the null hypothesis and the data are unusual, assuming the null hypothesis is true. If, however, the *p*-value is above .05, we can only conclude that the null hypothesis cannot be rejected, evidence against the null hypothesis was not found, or that a difference in group means could not be observed. Regardless of the observed *p*-value, it is more feasible to interpret evidence using CIs associated with the obtained effect size. We might obtain a mean difference of −2.0 units between groups in favor of the placebo procedure and the associated *p*-value is .4. Other suggestions include replacing the *p*-value with the surprisal value (S-value) or embracing the unconditional interpretation of statistical testing (2,16). **Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: A guide to misinterpretations**.

Learn more about how Pressbooks supports open publishing practices. # Chapter Two – Test Statistics, p Values, Confidence Intervals and Effect Sizes. Hello everyone, and welcome to the second chapter of the University of Southern Queensland’s online, open access textbook. The aim of this second chapter is to discuss three statistical tools that allow us to quickly determine if a given estimate of effect (or “effect size”) is statistically significant and if it may be of practical use: These tools are p Values and Confidence Intervals as well as the Effect Size itself. A p value is a statement of probability about how often a real association between variables would occur, and it is at the heart of the family of statistics based on frequencies of a particular event or outcome (in this case a real association between variables). Confidence intervals are another way of showing how useful an effect size estimate is, based on how much error has been added into making the estimate. Confidence intervals are important because they provide both an indication of statistical significance (that is, a real association between variables) for an effect as well as an indication of error in its estimation. Effect size estimates are important because they provide an indication of the magnitude of an effect, or how strong an association is between variables. There are some slides that appear via links within Chapter Two. Please look for these as you work your way through the current chapter. ## License. results.title: Statistical Significance Versus Clinical Importance of Observed Effect Sizes: What Do P Values and Confidence Intervals Really Represent? - PMC
results.content: # Statistical Significance Versus Clinical Importance of Observed Effect Sizes: What Do *P* Values and Confidence Intervals Really Represent? While null hypothesis significance testing is the predominant approach to statistical inference on effect sizes, results of such tests are often misinterpreted, provide no information on the magnitude of the estimate, and tell us nothing about the clinically importance of an effect. This tutorial reviews different effect size measures and describes how confidence intervals can be used to address not only the statistical significance but also the clinical significance of the observed effect or association. However, *P* values are often misinterpreted and provide no information on the magnitude or importance of the effect.1–3 Hence, rather than merely focusing on statistical significance, researchers should provide plausible estimates about the magnitude of the effect in the population from which the data were sampled.4,5. Previous statistical tutorials in this series initially discussed *P* values, confidence intervals (CIs), and effect size.6–8 The aim of the present basic statistical tutorial is to discuss in greater detail how a treatment effect or association can be quantified using the effect size, and how a CI can help to assess the statistical but especially also the clinical significance of the observed effect. The difference in mean temperature of 0.6°C was the observed point estimate of the magnitude of the treatment effect in the overall population of patients from which the sample was taken.6 We will discuss CIs below as a type of interval estimate of the observed effect size. The *P* value is the probability to observe a result at least as extreme as the one that was observed, under the assumption that the null hypothesis was actually true.1,2,21 Frey et al9 report a *P* value of <.001 for the difference in temperature between the groups. Note that there is a close relationship between CIs and significance testing.28 If the 95% CI of the effect size contains the value that indicates “no effect” (eg, the null value of 0 for a difference, or 1 for a risk ratio or odds ratio), this means that the data are compatible with no effect, corresponding to a nonsignificant result with a 0.05 significance cut-point level.

results.title: Confidence Intervals, p-Values and R-Software hdi
results.content: We present a (selective) review of recent frequentist high-dimensional inference methods for constructing p-values and conﬁdence intervals in linear and generalized linear models. The current paper has three main pillars: (i) a (selective) review of the development in frequentist high-dimensional inference methods for p-values and conﬁdence regions; (ii) presenting the ﬁrst broad, comparative empirical study among diﬀerent meth-ods, mainly for linear models: since the methods are mathematically justiﬁed under noncheckable and sometimes noncomparable assumptions, a thorough simulation study should lead to additional insights about reliability and performance of various pro-cedures; (iii) presenting the R-package hdi (high-dimensional inference) which enables to easily use many of the diﬀerent methods for inference in high-dimensional generalized linear models. HIGH-DIMENSIONAL INFERENCE: CONFIDENCE INTERVALS, P-VALUES AND R-SOFTWARE HDI 3 2.1 Diﬀerent Methods We describe here three diﬀerent methods for con-struction of statistical hypothesis tests or conﬁdence intervals. HIGH-DIMENSIONAL INFERENCE: CONFIDENCE INTERVALS, P-VALUES AND R-SOFTWARE HDI 11 2.5 A Broad Comparison We compare a variety of methods on the basis of multiple testing corrected p-values and single test-ing conﬁdence intervals. 3.1 Methods The Multi sample-splitting method can be modi-ﬁed for GLMs in an obvious way: the variable screen-ing step using the ﬁrst half of the data can be based on the ℓ1-norm regularized MLE, and p-values and conﬁdence intervals using the second half of the sam-ple are constructed from the asymptotic distribution of the (low-dimensional) MLE.
